ety.text: Inherited from Middle English deliberat(e), borrowed from Latin dēlīberātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīberō (“to consider, weigh well”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + *līberō / lībrō (“to weigh”)), from *libera / libra (“a balance”); see librate. Doublet of deliber.

senses.d: Done on purpose; intentional.
ex: a deliberate attempt to cover up his crime

senses.d: Formed with deliberation; carefully considered; not sudden or rash.
ex: a deliberate opinion; a deliberate measure or result
settled visage and deliberate word

senses.d: Of a person, weighing facts and arguments with a view to a choice or decision; carefully considering the probable consequences of a step; slow in determining.
ex: The jury took eight hours to come to its deliberate verdict.

senses.d: Not hasty or sudden; slow.
ex: His enunciation was so deliberate.

senses.d: To consider carefully; to weigh well in the mind.
ex: It is now time for the jury to deliberate the guilt of the defendant.

senses.d: To consider the reasons for and against anything; to reflect.

grp.label: of a person, carefully considering the probable consequences of a step
